paper_metadata.title: Natural vs programming language in LLM knowledge graph construction
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper studies knowledge-graph construction with smaller open-weight LLMs. Eight 7–8B models, plus 1B, 3B, and 70B variants, are fine-tuned with LoRA on ADE, CoNLL04, and SciERC using natural-language or Python-like prompts, optionally including chain-of-thought rationales. Prompt language has limited impact after fine-tuning, rationale training generally decreases performance, and smaller fine-tuned models can outperform the much larger closed-source CodeKGC baseline.

problem_addressed: The study addresses whether small, open-weight LLMs can perform RDF triple extraction for knowledge-graph construction as well as or better than larger closed-source models, and whether programming-language prompts improve structured extraction relative to natural-language prompts. It also examines the effects of chain-of-thought training and model size.

methodology.description: The system treats KGC as generative RDF triple extraction. For each dataset, the authors construct prompts in either natural language or Python-like code, optionally adding rationale lists that explicitly enumerate candidate entities and relations. Models receive three in-context examples and generate triples for a target sentence. The main experiments apply LoRA adapters to decoder attention and MLP modules while freezing the base model, using 200 training steps, batch size 8, learning rate 2×10^-4, and 42M trainable parameters for the 7–8B models. The study evaluates 175 model/settings combinations, including natural-language and code-pretrained models, instruction-tuned and completion models, model-size variants, no-fine-tuning controls, a 70B QLoRA condition, an ICL-example ablation, training-step analysis, attention visualizations, and LoRA-module ablations. The output is parsed/evaluated as exact RDF triples; no separate entity-recognition, linking, or graph-validation module is reported.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The method uses dataset-specific entity and relation schemas rather than discovering an ontology. In code prompts, generic Rel, Entity, Triple, and Extract classes are combined with dataset-specific subclasses such as Adverse_effect, Drug, and Disease. The natural-language prompts also instruct the model to produce the target RDF-triple format. No external ontology, entity-linking knowledge base, or schema induction procedure is reported.

evidence.excerpt: Relations and entities can be represented as the classes Rel and Entity, and each relation and entity type can be represented as a sub-class.
The schema defines general classes for relations (Rel) and entities (Entity), along with classes specific to the dataset.

text_to_kg_stages: Input sentence/document presentation to the LLM; no separate preprocessing stage is reported.
Entity and concept extraction through generative prediction of entity strings.
Entity typing through dataset-specific entity classes in the generated triples and code schema.
Relation and triple extraction as the central task.
Graph construction as RDF-style triples of the form (entity, relation, entity).
Coreference resolution is not separately solved or evaluated; SciERC contains coreference annotations, but the reported evaluation is exact triple extraction.
Entity resolution/linking, ontology discovery, knowledge fusion, deduplication, graph validation/correction, and graph updating are not reported as separate stages.

input_output.input_type: Unstructured natural-language text from medical case reports, news articles, and scientific literature.
input_output.input_granularity: Primarily sentence-level or short text-instance inputs, with examples and target outputs formatted in prompts; the paper evaluates benchmark instances rather than complete documents or deployed graphs.
input_output.output_representation: Exact RDF-style triples represented as ordered textual triples [subject, relation, object], with code-prompt variants wrapped in Python-like classes such as Extract([Triple(...)]).

models_and_tools: LoRA; QLoRA and bitsandbytes for 70B models; AdamW optimizer; cross-entropy language-model loss
datasets: ADE: medical adverse-drug-effect corpus; CodeKGC subset, 2,562/300 documents and 4,087/452 entity/relation instances.
CoNLL04: news-domain relation-extraction corpus; 922/288 documents with five relation types and four entity types.
SciERC: scientific-literature corpus; 1,366/397 documents with six entity types, seven relation types, and coreference annotations.
The study uses the same sub-sampled train/test splits created for CodeKGC.

metrics: Exact triple match: a triple counts as correct only when subject, relation, and object all exactly match the gold triple.
Three testing runs averaged for the main model comparisons; five runs for the LoRA-module ablation.
baselines: Instruction-tuned open-weight models evaluated without fine-tuning
Full fine-tuning and partial LoRA-module variants in the ablation study
evaluation.setting: Supervised fine-tuning and inference on the CodeKGC sub-sampled train/test splits for ADE, CoNLL04, and SciERC. Training uses three randomly sampled in-context examples plus a target example, 200 steps, batch size 8, and no validation-based checkpoint selection. Each model is evaluated directly on the test set, generally in three repeated runs, using strict exact-triple matching. Additional experiments vary model size, prompt language, rationale use, number of ICL examples, training steps, and LoRA target modules.

value: Experimental result: the best fine-tuned models achieve micro-F1 0.812 on ADE, 0.705 on CoNLL04, and 0.396 on SciERC; the best ADE and CoNLL04 results are from Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, while Mistral-7B-v0.3 obtains the best SciERC result.

Experimental result: compared with CodeKGC, the paper reports improvements of 17.4 F1 points on ADE, 19.7 on CoNLL04, and 15.5 on SciERC in the abstract; the discussion reports approximately 17, 20.9, and 14.9 points for the selected best comparisons.

Experimental result: prompt language has limited impact after fine-tuning; only 5 of 12 best results for code-pretrained LLMs use code prompts, and natural-language prompts are slightly better overall.

Experimental result: rationale/chain-of-thought training lowers performance for all fine-tuned models except one. For Mistral-7B-v0.3 on SciERC, the no-rationale score is 0.396 versus 0.357 with rationale.
Experimental result: fine-tuned 1B and 3B Llama models outperform the fine-tuned 70B Llama models under the same limited-data setup, while the 70B base model is stronger than smaller base models.
Experimental result: across all fine-tuned and base models, mean micro-F1 is 0.719 versus 0.192 on ADE, 0.582 versus 0.087 on CoNLL04, and 0.305 versus 0.032 on SciERC.

Review-level interpretation: the experiments support the claim that task-specific adaptation and output-format supervision mattered more than pre-training size or code specialization under this small-data regime.

value: Author claim: the approach uses open-weight models, enabling inspection of model behavior and more stable reproducibility than changing online APIs.
Experimental strength: LoRA adaptation provides large gains with only 42M trainable parameters for 7–8B models and a small 200-step training budget.
Experimental strength: the study systematically varies prompt language, rationale use, model pre-training domain, model size, number of ICL examples, training steps, and LoRA modules.
Experimental strength: the strict exact-triple metric gives a conservative measure of simultaneous subject, relation, and object correctness.
Review-level interpretation: the common datasets and shared CodeKGC splits make the prompt and model-size comparisons internally coherent.

evidence.excerpt: Using open-weight models is essential because only by having access to the weights can one analyze the behavior of a model.
each model has 42M trainable parameters.

value: Experimental weakness: the approach predicts raw textual triples and does not report separate entity linking, coreference resolution, ontology discovery, graph validation, deduplication, or graph updating components.

Experimental weakness: the strict exact-match metric penalizes harmless punctuation, spacing, or adjective differences; the error analysis shows predictions that are semantically plausible but counted as wrong.
Experimental weakness: no validation-set model selection is performed, and most experiments use only 200 training steps and 1,600 observed training examples per setting.

Experimental weakness: performance is substantially lower on specialized SciERC than on ADE or CoNLL04, with errors involving technical relations, entity order, and long-distance/coreferential dependencies.
Review-level interpretation: comparisons are limited to three benchmark datasets and may not establish robustness for heterogeneous, document-level, multilingual, or production KG construction.

value: The 70B models cannot be fairly fully explored because the available hardware did not permit 16-bit or 8-bit LoRA tuning; the 70B experiments therefore use 4-bit quantization.
The 4K context limit of deepseek-coder-7b-base-v1.5 prevents experiments with 15 or more ICL examples.
The limited 1,600-example training regime may be insufficient to steer 70B models and may explain why smaller models outperform them after fine-tuning.
The authors do not pursue additional 70B training because it would conflict with the goal of reducing compute requirements and was computationally infeasible.
The authors note that future work should test more data and training steps for larger models, lighter non-LLM models, and RAG-derived information during prompt training.

value: Whether larger open-weight models can outperform smaller models when given sufficient domain-specific fine-tuning data remains unresolved.
The study does not resolve how to reliably extract technically complex relations and long-distance/coreferential dependencies in SciERC-like scientific text.
The effect of code versus natural-language prompting under larger datasets, different schemas, and broader domains remains unresolved.
The paper leaves open whether RAG-based domain information during prompt training is better than domain-relevant pre-training.
Exact triple generation remains vulnerable to entity-boundary, punctuation, entity-order, relation-direction, and semantically plausible but annotation-incompatible errors.
